title: Unit Tests for Benefit Law: Eligibility System Conformance
one_liner: Invert the drill: aim the same synthetic households and adjudicated answer keys at the eligibility software itself, selling H.R.1 conformance test packs to states and system vendors, with an aim to become the standard test suite that state RFPs cite.
customer: State SNAP and Medicaid policy directors and eligibility-system program managers (the people running user-acceptance testing), then the system integrators that build the systems and the AI-tool vendors selling into agencies. First buyers: 2-3 states whose H.R.1 system releases are due between Oct 2026 and Jan 2027 and that already have a UAT process.
problem: The most expensive error is one the system makes identically thousands of times, which no worker training can fix. NC's eligibility system stacked shelter deductions when caseworkers updated rent, and a one-click prompt fixed it and has since been used more than 20,000 times. H.R.1 forces reprogramming everywhere at once (SNAP work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance rules, Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals due around Jan 2027) under a 75% state admin share and a 6% error cliff. Vendors test their own work. States rarely have independent, boundary-case test data with signed-off expected outcomes.
solution: H.R.1 Conformance Pack v1: about 250 synthetic households aimed at the edges of each changed rule (income at the threshold, mixed-status households, month-boundary changes, shelter and utility interactions), each with an expected outcome and a citation trail to statute, USDA guidance and the state manual. The state's own policy staff sign off the answer key, so we test state policy against state system and do not have to settle federal ambiguity. Where state policy and federal guidance conflict, we flag it as a second deliverable, a QC-risk memo. Delivery fits existing UAT: scenario scripts and machine-readable fixtures with expected results, plus a divergence report. Later: a regression subscription refreshed on every guidance change, vendor pre-certification, and household-level evaluation sets for AI intake and caseworker-assist tools.
why_now: Every state must change its SNAP and Medicaid eligibility logic within months of each other, and Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals land around Jan 2027. AI tools are entering benefits workflows and agencies have no household-level ground truth to test them against. USDA's FY2025 numbers (41 states above 6%, 10.62% nationally) make a systemic logic bug politically and financially radioactive. Open-source rules engines (PolicyEngine) and LLM-assisted drafting cut the cost of building cases, so adjudication, not authoring, is now the scarce step.
revenue_model: Per-state pack at $40-120k per major rule change, and a regression subscription at $100-250k a year per program per state. Vendor certification runs at $15-50k and AI-tool evaluation runs at $10-30k. Bottom-up: 50 states x 3 programs x about $300k, so $30-60M ARR is a plausible ceiling, and more if state RFPs cite the suite as an acceptance criterion. Much of the spend can draw federal IT matching funds in system-change budgets (verify per program). Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Independence is the product, in the way UL or a ratings agency is. Vendors cannot credibly grade their own homework, and states cannot staff independent test authorship, so the cornered resource is the adjudicated, state-signed answer key: expert time that compounds across states and rule changes. Testing the machine reaches a bigger error source than training people, and the same answer-key corpus later powers worker drills, QC calibration and AI evaluation. A standard is reachable because states already buy test scripts and would rather cite a neutral suite than write their own.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 12 H.R.1 SNAP provisions from USDA implementation memos and write 60 boundary-case households. Run them through PolicyEngine and through 2-3 states' public online benefit screeners, which needs no system access. Days 10-18: send each state policy director a private divergence report with 3-5 mismatches and an offer of the full pack. Days 15-30: sign 1-2 paid $25-40k UAT-pack pilots with a state policy or IT lead, and start talks with a system integrator's state account team about pre-certification. Recruit 2 ex-state policy and ex-FNS adjudicators to sign keys.
lineage: mutation of I1240 ('Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Maximus - Accuracy Assistant (SNAP solutions), Code for America - Social Safety Net / SNAP programs, Kognito (sunset) - conversation simulation training, PolicyEngine (open-source US benefit rules engine) and related SNAP repos. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget ran out before I could run any searches, so this is a partial check. It rests on direct fetches of about 15 URLs (the idea's cited sources, Maximus, PCG, PSI, Code for America, Kognito, Relias, Deloitte, Route Fifty) plus GitHub repo searches. Several sites returned 403, 404 or 503. It could not cover Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC or TechCrunch, or find startup names. The absence of a found direct competitor is therefore weaker than a full search would give, and should be re-checked with searches such as 'SNAP eligibility worker training simulation', 'benefits caseworker AI roleplay startup', and 'eligibility training' RFPs before the founder commits.

What looks unserved: (1) No product I found gives eligibility workers a daily, scored, synthetic-case drill tied to the specific federal QC error elements (wages, household composition, shelter and address changes) with per-worker error-type heatmaps. Maximus's Accuracy Assistant explicitly works 'side-by-side' in live cases and does not train. Code for America and PolicyEngine are systems and rules tools. Kognito-style simulation vendors never targeted eligibility work. (2) Nothing found ties practice performance to documented CQI or corrective-action-plan evidence, which NC's official explicitly asks counties for ('documenting, documenting, documenting'). (3) New-hire ramp-up: Kansas cited turnover and caseworker training complexity as drivers of its errors, and no product measures time-to-competency.

The main threats are structural rather than competitive: (a) the real buyer is the state, which typically owns training (state academies, mandated curricula, training environments in the state eligibility system), and county discretionary budgets may not cover $12k-25k; (b) Maximus or a state's existing LMS vendor could add a practice module; (c) policy variation across states (BBCE, standard utility allowance, county practices) makes per-state case libraries costly to build and keep current; (d) an open-source rules engine (PolicyEngine) lowers the barrier for copycats. | How this version avoids them: Maximus Accuracy Assistant scores live cases for risk and does not test system logic. Code for America and Nava help states build and communicate rules, not produce independent conformance suites. PolicyEngine is the natural supplier and partner (open-source engine, nonprofit, no state-signed answer keys or sales motion), and its SNAP screener validation is not a state-system acceptance test. Vals AI's Public Benefits Bench (with Code for America and the Center for Civic Futures) is a proprietary question-answering benchmark for beneficiary inquiries. It does not test household eligibility or benefit calculations, so we supply the household-level layer and could partner. System vendors and IV&V firms test their own or generic project deliverables, and independence is our counter-position. The Kognito failure is irrelevant here because the buyer is a funded IT/UAT process, not a training budget. State academies are not substitutes.

competitors.name: Maximus - Accuracy Assistant (SNAP solutions)
competitors.what_they_do: AI-powered, human-in-the-loop tool that pre-scores cases for error risk from historical error data and state rules, flags high-risk cases before benefits issue, guides workers through interviews and documentation gaps. Marketed on maximus.com as 'Reduce SNAP error rates and case backlogs.' Texas and Wisconsin are referenced. It works alongside staff in the live workflow and is NOT a skills-training or synthetic-case drill product, but it is the closest incumbent already selling 'error reduction' to state agencies and could bolt on a training module.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Public company (NYSE: MMS), multi-billion-dollar revenue (figure from memory, not verified on fetch); pricing not published.

competitors.name: Code for America - Social Safety Net / SNAP programs
competitors.what_they_do: Nonprofit that works with state agencies on SNAP application flow, automation and AI-assisted case processing, and published a Work Requirements Implementation Toolkit. The fetched page shows no caseworker training, error-rate drills or case-review product.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Large philanthropy-funded nonprofit; sells no per-seat training product that I could find.

competitors.name: Kognito (sunset) - conversation simulation training
competitors.what_they_do: Ran role-play simulations for mental-health training, mainly in schools and higher ed. The site says the brand is being sunset, with all selling and marketing stopped as of Aug 2023. It never served eligibility work as far as the fetched page shows. It is a cautionary data point: simulation-based training for public-sector staff was a hard business to sustain.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Defunct or winding down; not a live competitor.

competitors.name: PolicyEngine (open-source US benefit rules engine) and related SNAP repos
competitors.what_they_do: Open-source engine that computes SNAP eligibility and benefits. It is not a training product, but it lowers the cost of building a scoring engine and could be used by others to generate synthetic cases. TheAxiomFoundation/finbot-snap-demo (https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/finbot-snap-demo) is a Colorado SNAP rules chatbot demo built on it. GitHub searches for SNAP caseworker training simulators, QC error-rate training and synthetic-case tools returned no repositories.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Nonprofit-backed open source; the demo repos have 0 stars.

competitors.name: State-run eligibility training academies, LMS and training regions, plus USDA FNS QC resources (unverified)
competitors.what_they_do: Many states already train workers through in-house academies, university partners and practice cases in a training copy of the eligibility system. NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeted CQI training for high-error counties. Maryland and Virginia are revamping training, and Virginia issued an executive order for new local department training. USDA FNS publishes free payment-accuracy resources. The FNS page returned 403 and I could not verify its content, so this rests on the state-action reporting cited below and on background knowledge. It is the real substitute product the drills must beat.

competitors.name: Big-consultancy SNAP payment-accuracy practices (PCG, Policy Studies Inc, Deloitte and similar) - unverified
competitors.what_they_do: These firms sell error-rate reduction consulting, QC case reviews and corrective-action-plan support to states. I could not confirm a specific SNAP product. The PCG homepage showed no SNAP QC offering, PCG's payment-accuracy page redirected to a 404, and the Policy Studies Inc site returned 503. Kansas hired an unnamed outside consultant. These firms compete for the same state budget as the idea's proposed 'second-look review desk' add-on, not for the drills.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established, multi-hundred-million-dollar consultancies; status unverified for SNAP specifically.

I1240.evidence_of_demand:
Strong on the problem side, unproven on 'will pay for a training product'.

Problem is real and funded by law. NCPR confirms St. Lawrence County's extra cost of $776,000 (rising to about $1M the next year), Jefferson County at over $1M, Warren County at $415,000, about $168M extra statewide in admin costs, and NY's 13% error rate against the 6% line with about a $1B penalty from October 2027 (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind). That article says nothing about counties buying training, vendors or tools, so it shows pain, not purchase intent.

States are visibly spending on error reduction, per the reporting at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html. Louisiana (7.61%, about $100M exposure) pays cash bonuses for spotting errors and has intensified case reviews. Kansas (nearly 10% down to a reported 5.5%) hired an outside consultant and cites turnover and training complexity. Maryland (over 13%, about $240M) is revamping training. Virginia (11.5%, about $270M) issued an executive order for new local-department training, is partnering with unnamed tech companies and is consulting experts. Mississippi (over 10%) is buying case-management software and training staff. No dollar amounts or vendor names were given for these.

NC's DSS official cites 'updated policy and targeted training' and CQI support aimed at high-error counties, monthly QC webinars, revised interview guides piloted in Catawba, Duplin and Forsyth, NC FAST automation wizards and intelligent document-processing pilots. She also asked counties to report barriers and low uptake of the tools (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares). This shows the state is building its own webinars and tools, which is competing free supply.

Vendors are pursuing the same budget: Maximus markets 'Reduce SNAP error rates and case backlogs' with its Accuracy Assistant (https://maximus.com/state-and-local-government/snap), which shows commercial demand for error reduction but in a workflow-tool form.

Not found: any RFP, county budget line, or forum complaint showing counties paying per-worker for drill-style training, or any published price benchmarks. The idea's $150-300 per worker and $12k-25k per county prices are unvalidated assumptions.
I1240.sharper_angle:
Drop the 'per-county SaaS' framing and sell a state-level continuous-quality-improvement (CQI) evidence and onboarding layer that complements, rather than competes with, workflow tools like Maximus's Accuracy Assistant.

1. Buyer and wedge. Sell to the state SNAP office or county association, since counties are penalized by the state average. Start with one state that already runs county-targeted CQI (NC is the obvious one, given its monthly QC webinars and named high-error counties). Offer a pilot for the high-error counties the state has already identified.

2. Build the case library from the state's own de-identified QC findings and corrective-action-plan error categories, not just the generic USDA taxonomy. Start with the two or three elements that drive most errors (earned income and wage calculation from pay stubs, household composition and address changes, shelter deductions). Using the state's own findings is the moat a generic vendor or open-source rules engine can't copy quickly.

3. Sell documentation, not just skill. Each drill produces a per-worker, per-county audit trail (pre and post scores, error-type trends, time-to-competency for new hires) that the county can attach to its CQI or corrective-action documentation. NC's official is explicitly asking for that documentation.

4. Position at the new-hire and turnover problem (cited by Kansas) as a 30-day onboarding accelerator with a measurable pre/post result, rather than a daily-forever habit, which is easier to justify against the free state academy.

5. Partner rather than fight the incumbent. Maximus flags risky cases in-workflow and does not train workers. Offer drills as a complementary skill-building layer, or accept Maximus or a state-system vendor as an eventual acquirer or channel.

6. De-risk before building. Run real searches (Crunchbase, Product Hunt, YC, procurement portals, state RFP sites) to confirm no funded 'caseworker training simulator' exists, and get one county director or state CQI lead to say what they would pay and from which budget line before writing 40 cases.
